policy: Every capability records its assets, its trust zones, the boundaries between them, the STRIDE threats on those boundaries and the repository artefacts that mitigate them. A claim is only accepted when it points at something real: an asset names a source (a path in this repository, or a binding NAME), a node names the file it claims to be, and every control and mitigation is a path that exists or a command a release actually runs. The ledger describes assets by name and never by value — no credential, no binding value and no production secret is recorded here or printed by the gate that reads this file.

control_registry.contract: Proves the two CSRF layers stay separate: the framework default guards `/_serverFn/*` and `csrfGuard` guards `/api/v1/*`, with no path that reaches neither.
Proves the declared Cloudflare surface the code depends on still matches the configuration, including the rate-limit bindings that bound abuse on the boundary and the login path.
Proves the framing policy of the shipped documents: which surfaces may be framed, which may never be, and that no `public/` document is left without a rule.
Proves each Tool's declared license and dependency set match the reviewed inventory record, so a Tool artefact cannot drift from what was reviewed.
Proves a vendored build input comes from the reviewed checkout at the recorded revision, so a build cannot consume an unreviewed source.
Proves the published state of the portfolio content matches the owner's decision surface, so a content change cannot reach the public surface unreviewed.
Runs the outbound URL policy over its destination matrix and exits non-zero when a measurement contradicts the outcome its row claims, which is the machine half of the egress policy.
Reads the media bucket key set status-only and fails when a key exists outside the public prefixes, which is the enforcement half of the media visibility policy.
Scans the tracked tree and the build output for credential shapes so a value cannot be committed or bundled, which is the machine half of the secret source-of-truth rule.
Proves every secret name the Wrangler configuration declares is covered by the Infisical inventory and by its environment separation, without reading any value.

capabilities.title: External HTTP boundary (/api/v1/*)
capabilities.owner: the external HTTP boundary obligation in `src/http/**`, mounted by the Worker entry `src/server.ts`
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §2/§3 — `http` owns the inbound external boundary and its own CSRF layer; the split from TanStack Start is enforced in `src/server.ts`
capabilities.summary: Every request that did not come from the TanStack Start UI is answered here, so the caller is untrusted until a key, an origin and a rate budget say otherwise.

assets.description: The consumer API key a self-consuming client presents on the boundary; only its hash is stored, and the plaintext never enters the repository.
The D1 rows behind the access counter and its increment path, readable through the boundary and writable through the access router.
The DB-backed emoji catalog and its slug grammar, which the reactions and reaction-image routes read and the boundary scopes per action.
The unauthenticated documents this boundary serves — health, db/r2 pings, the security-txt and crawler documents — including the release version they publish.
Operator-visible log records the boundary writes through the redacting logger, carrying a correlation id and the values redacted before they are written.

boundaries.crosses: The inbound external boundary: an arbitrary request with its own headers enters the Worker and must be authenticated, origin-checked and rate-bounded before any handler runs.
The D1 trust boundary: a value validated at the edge becomes a parameter-bound statement against the database binding.
The operator-visibility boundary: an internal failure becomes a redacted log record plus a correlation id, never a value in the response.

threats.scenario: A caller presents a guessed or replayed consumer key to act with the authority of the self-consuming client, and the boundary cannot tell the forgery from the real key.

mitigations.note: The middleware compares the presented key against the stored hash and refuses an unknown key with a stable code before any handler runs.
The suite asserts the accepted key, the missing header, the unknown key and the wrong-shape key cases.

threats.scenario: A key issued for the read scope calls a write action and is allowed through because authentication is treated as authorisation.

mitigations.note: Resource and action scopes are checked separately from key validity and a missing scope is a 403, not a 500.
The resource/action matrix is documented per route so a new route states its scope.

threats.scenario: A third-party page makes the browser issue a credentialed write to `/api/v1/*`, changing public state from an origin the user never visited for that purpose.

mitigations.note: Unsafe methods are origin-checked with fetch-metadata, Origin and Referer, and a request with none of them is refused.
The gate proves the boundary layer and the framework layer each keep their own check.

threats.scenario: A shared cache serves one caller's response to another because the boundary answers with credentials and did not vary on them.

mitigations.note: Every boundary response is a function of the caller's identity unless a handler explicitly opts into public caching with a positive freshness lifetime.
The suite asserts the isolation headers across the credentialed and public-read routes.

threats.scenario: An internal failure is answered with the exception, the SQL or the binding name, so a caller learns the shape of the datastore from an error message.

mitigations.note: Failures answer with a stable code, a repo-authored message and the correlation id only.
The gate keeps `console.*` behind the redacting logger, so the record is written through one policy.

threats.scenario: A caller floods a write endpoint until the database binding is the only thing standing between the flood and the rest of the site.

mitigations.note: Write and read budgets are enforced per principal with a Retry-After on refusal.
The gate keeps the rate-limit bindings the code reads declared in the Cloudflare configuration.

review_items: Does every route added under `/api/v1/*` appear in the resource/action scope matrix, or is a new action shipping with an inherited scope?
Is any response on this boundary still cacheable by a shared cache without `Vary: Origin` and the caller-identity headers?
Can a failure on this boundary still name a binding, a table or a secret in the body it returns?

capabilities.title: Authentication and Admin session boundary
capabilities.owner: the auth route obligation `src/http/auth/**` with the Admin loaders in `src/admin/**`
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §3 — `/api/v1/auth/*` is Better Auth behind the boundary; the Admin surface reads it through server functions and its own redirect policy
capabilities.summary: A browser holds a session cookie that becomes an Admin capability, so the crossing is judged by origin, by redirect target and by step-up freshness rather than by the cookie alone.

assets.description: The Better Auth session cookie that stands for an authenticated identity on every Admin request.
What the session unlocks: emoji catalog edits, image management, key and invitation administration.
The post-login destination the login loader accepts from the query string and the boundary classifies before following it.

boundaries.crosses: The authentication crossing: a cookie-carrying write from a browser must be same-origin and must reach only trusted origins.
The authorisation crossing: an authenticated browser becomes an Admin capability, and the step-up state decides how much of it is available.
The navigation crossing: a caller-supplied return target must be classified before any redirect is emitted.

threats.scenario: A login link carries an absolute or protocol-relative return target, so the site hands the browser to an origin the attacker chose with the user's session in the URL bar.

mitigations.note: The boundary classifier refuses anything that is not a same-origin path, and the login route additionally restricts the accepted prefixes.
The browser test walks the accepted and refused return targets through the real login screen.

threats.scenario: An attacker replays leaked credentials at the login endpoint until a human account is locked out or the endpoint is saturated.

mitigations.note: The login path is inside the read budget and refuses with a Retry-After.
The gate keeps the rate-limit bindings this path reads declared in the Cloudflare configuration.
The enumeration contract records that a refusal never distinguishes an unknown account from a wrong password.

threats.scenario: An authenticated but not recently verified session reaches a destructive Admin action, so possession of an old cookie is enough to change published state.

mitigations.note: The sensitive actions read the step-up state and refuse a session that is not fresh enough.
The suite asserts both the stale and the fresh session for each guarded action.

threats.scenario: A logout leaves the session usable, so an action taken afterwards cannot be attributed to a session the user believes they ended.

mitigations.note: The suite asserts that the cookie is invalidated server-side, not only cleared in the browser.
The cookie contract is a single declaration both the runtime and the tests read.

review_items: Does every new Admin action declare whether it needs step-up, and is that decision visible in the route rather than inside the loader?
Is any new query parameter able to influence where the browser is sent after login without passing the redirect classifier?
Can a refusal on this surface be used to distinguish an unknown account from a wrong password?

capabilities.title: Portfolio publication surface (authored content)
capabilities.owner: the portfolio obligation in `src/portfolio/**`, including the publication loader and the Markdown input boundary
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §3 — `portfolio` owns the employment-facing data model and publication contract; the owner approves what is published
capabilities.summary: Authored Markdown and owner-selected rows become a public document, so the crossing is the loader and the input boundary that decides what is stored and what is rendered.

assets.description: The D1 rows behind each project entry, including the owner-selected ordering and the publication flag that decides visibility.
Authored article bodies derived from an external editor and stored as Markdown or HTML, sanitised on the way in and lexed on the way out.
The public project list and article pages, including the structured data projected from the same rows.

boundaries.crosses: The authored-content input boundary: text copied from an external editor becomes stored content, so raw HTML and link targets must be decided before storage.
The visibility boundary: a row becomes public only because the owner selected it, and the filter that enforces that lives with the portfolio obligation.

threats.scenario: A payload carried in imported article content survives into the rendered document and executes for every visitor of the public article page.

mitigations.note: Raw HTML is rendered as escaped text and a refused link keeps its reason without becoming an anchor.
The browser test asserts the payload never fires on the real page.

threats.scenario: A row that the owner never selected reaches the public index because the loader forgot the visibility filter on one code path.

mitigations.note: The public loader returns only published rows and nothing else is exported for the public surface.
The suite asserts that an unpublished row is absent from the list, the article and the structured data.
The publication diff is what the owner reads to decide what changes state, so an unintended publication is a visible diff.

threats.scenario: The public loader is changed into a per-row query, so a page that used to cost one statement now costs one per project on every visit.

mitigations.note: The query-budget test fails when the loader's statement count grows past the recorded budget.
The loader is a DI seam, so the statement count is asserted against a fake and not only against D1.

review_items: Is every field that reaches a public project page still passing through the lexer, or has a new field been rendered as text directly?
Does any new publication path read the portfolio tables without the owner-selection filter?
Has the query budget for the public loader been re-checked since the last content-shape change?

capabilities.title: Media storage visibility (R2 MEDIA bucket)
capabilities.owner: the Cloudflare runtime obligation `src/cloudflare/media-visibility.ts`, applied by the upload paths that use it
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §4 — the `MEDIA` binding is declared in the Wrangler configuration; the public-prefix policy is the enforcement owner's decision
capabilities.summary: One bucket holds both published images and unpublished uploads, so the crossing is the visibility classifier every read and every upload has to pass.

assets.description: Objects under the published prefixes, served from the public custom domain without a signature.
Reaction images and Admin uploads that are not published yet and must never resolve through the public domain.
The key set of the production bucket, read status-only by the release-time audit that decides whether a key exists outside the public prefixes.

boundaries.crosses: The upload crossing: a caller-supplied image reference becomes an object in a bucket that also serves published media.
The public read crossing: an object resolves through the public custom domain only when its key is inside the published prefixes.

threats.scenario: An upload lands in a key namespace the public domain serves, so an unpublished Admin or reaction image becomes readable by anyone holding the URL.

mitigations.note: The classifier runs its deny list before the allow list, so a key in both lists resolves to private.
The audit reads the production key set status-only and fails when a key exists outside the public prefixes.

threats.scenario: A caller submits an image reference that points at an existing object under a published prefix, so a write path adopts or re-publishes someone else's object.

mitigations.note: The suite rejects references whose shape, prefix or namespace is not the one the caller owns.
The portfolio media module applies the same policy for its own composition.

threats.scenario: Uploads accumulate in the bucket with no owner, so the key set grows without bound and the release-time audit stops being a decision anyone can act on.

mitigations.note: The runbook records the audit as a release step with its own verdict vocabulary.
The gate fails closed on anything it cannot decide, so an unreadable key set is not a pass.

review_items: Does any new upload path write a key outside the published prefixes without recording it as a deliberate exception?
Is the public read path still the only one that can resolve an object without a signature?
Has a key been added to the published prefixes since the last release-time audit run?

capabilities.title: Tool shell and third-party artefact embed
capabilities.owner: the Tool Registry obligation in `src/tools/**` with the framing policy in `src/http/security-headers.ts`
capabilities.authority: ADR-0006 — a Tool is a reviewed manifest plus a separate artefact repository; the embed policy is the Tool Registry's own contract
capabilities.summary: A Tool artefact is third-party code the site frames, so the crossing is the shell route and the iframe sandbox that decides what the framed document may reach.

assets.description: The Tool manifest that declares a Tool's version, licence, outbound targets and embed delivery policy.
The artefact a Tool serves, built from a reviewed checkout of the Tools repository and checked against the recorded inventory.
What the shell document can reach — the session cookie, the Admin routes and the API boundary — which a framed document must not inherit.

boundaries.crosses: The framing crossing: a third-party document may only be rendered by a policy that decided the sandbox tokens and the capability grants first.
The shell crossing: what the manifest decided is what the route renders, so the artefact's reach over the host page is the policy's answer and nothing else.

threats.scenario: A third-party page frames an Admin or Tool document and induces a click the user believes they made elsewhere.

mitigations.note: The framing policy is bound per path in the Worker entry and in the static rules, and the gate refuses a rule opened to `*`.
The gate reads the shipped rules and four deliberately broken fixtures, so a widened rule fails.

threats.scenario: A framed Tool artefact is granted `allow-same-origin`, so its document runs on the site's own origin and reads whatever the shell exposes.

mitigations.note: `allow-same-origin` is rejected for every framed Tool, and a capability grant needs an explicit allow-list plus a written rationale.
The policy test asserts the rejected token set and the missing-rationale cases.

threats.scenario: The artefact served for a reviewed Tool changes after review, so the site ships code whose licence, dependency set and outbound targets nobody approved.

mitigations.note: The declared licence is checked against the pinned checkout and the dependency set against the reviewed record; missing evidence is an error.
The Tools repository provenance is checked so a Tool cannot come from an unreviewed checkout.

review_items: Does a new Tool declare `delivery.iframe` explicitly, or is it inheriting an implicit default the policy forbids?
Can any Tool artefact reach the Admin routes or the API boundary with the shell's own origin?
Has the reviewed inventory record been updated in the same change as the Tool manifest?

capabilities.title: Outbound third-party read (external-api)
capabilities.owner: the outbound read obligation `src/external-api/**` with the URL policy `src/http/outbound.ts`
capabilities.authority: ADR-0002 / `docs/domain/integrations.md` — an outbound read is not an `http/**` concern; capability-scoped first, and nothing is mounted on a route yet
capabilities.summary: A display component may read a third-party API, so the crossing is the URL policy and the single place an outbound request is issued; no route mounts it yet.

assets.description: The third-party endpoint a snapshot is read from, constrained by the outbound URL policy before a request is issued.
The last successful snapshot a card renders while the reader is failing, including how old it may be before it stops being shown.

boundaries.crosses: The egress crossing: a caller-supplied or manifest-declared URL is resolved and connected only after the policy classifies it.
The presentation crossing: a bounded, stale-aware snapshot becomes a rendered card, and a failure degrades without destroying the last good value.

threats.scenario: A URL that resolves to an internal address or a link-local metadata endpoint is fetched from the Worker, so a third-party read becomes an internal probe.

mitigations.note: The classifier refuses private, loopback, link-local and non-HTTP(S) targets before a connection is opened.
The policy test walks the refused matrix: scheme, credentials, private ranges and encoded forms.
The destination matrix fails the run when a measurement contradicts the outcome its row claims, so the refusals stay live.

threats.scenario: A third party that stops answering holds the render open, so the page depends on someone else's uptime instead of degrading to the last snapshot.

mitigations.note: One place issues the request and it is bounded by an attempt budget and a per-attempt timeout.
The contract test asserts the breaker opens and that the fallback is non-destructive.
Wiring the reader to a route is the remaining hand-work; nothing is mounted on a route today.

threats.follow_up: Decide whether any route mounts the reader, and record the decision before a snapshot can become reachable at runtime.

review_items: Is any route able to reach the outbound reader today, and if not, does the UI still render as if a live snapshot exists?
Does a new outbound call go through the single fetch seam, or has a second one appeared next to it?
Does the stale snapshot carry an age the reader can see, rather than presenting an old value as current?

capabilities.title: Runtime secret delivery (Infisical to the Worker)
capabilities.owner: the Cloudflare runtime obligation `src/cloudflare/auth/**` with the Infisical source-of-truth contract in ADR-0015
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §4 and ADR-0015 — Infisical holds the values, the Wrangler configuration declares only the names, and Cloudflare Workers Builds performs the deploy
capabilities.summary: A value never enters the repository; the pipeline reads it at release time and binds it to the Worker, so the crossing is the release job rather than a request.

assets.description: The runtime secret values held in Infisical and bound to the Worker; this ledger names the bindings and never their contents.
The names the Wrangler configuration declares as required, which is the source-controlled half of the contract.
The consumer API key the release pipeline uses to reach Infisical, scoped for the release environment only.

boundaries.crosses: The release boundary: an unreviewed change must not be able to make the pipeline read or publish a value on its way to production.
The binding boundary: names declared in the configuration must match the names Infisical covers, in the right environment, before the deploy.

threats.scenario: A credential shape is committed or lands in a build artefact, so the repository or its published output becomes the leak instead of Infisical.

mitigations.note: The tree and the build output are scanned for credential shapes, and a finding fails the run.
Runtime logging masks values before they reach a record, so a log line cannot become the second copy.

threats.scenario: The configuration declares a binding nobody provisions, or one Infisical covers that the Worker no longer declares, so the release looks complete while the runtime binding is missing.

mitigations.note: The coverage check compares declared names with the inventory status-only and fails on a mismatch.
The comparison script emits MATCH / DIFFER / MISSING and never prints the value it compared.

threats.scenario: An automation path merges the release PR or publishes the tag without the owner's approval, so a deploy happens outside the approval the runbook makes mandatory.

mitigations.note: The release sequence records the human approval gate and the order the steps must run in.
Workflow actions are pinned, so a deploy step cannot be redirected by an upstream tag moving.

review_items: Is every binding a new Worker route reads already declared in the configuration and covered by the inventory?
Does any new script, report or screenshot risk printing a value where only a name is needed?
Has a rotation changed a name rather than a value, and does the release sequence still match the runbook?

capabilities.title: Build and dependency supply chain
capabilities.owner: the repository's release-integrity obligation: the workflow pins, the SBOM, the advisory gate and the artefact attestation
capabilities.authority: AGENTS.md §5 and `docs/security/supply-chain-*.md` — validation is owned by GitHub Actions; production delivery is owned by Cloudflare Workers Builds
capabilities.summary: The build reads third-party code and third-party actions, so the crossing is the pinned reference plus the record of what was built and reviewed.

assets.description: The pinned dependency tree and the SBOM generated from it, which is what an advisory verdict and a provenance claim are made against.
The third-party actions every workflow runs, pinned to an immutable reference so a moved tag cannot change a release step.
The attestation manifest linking a built artefact to the inputs that produced it.

boundaries.crosses: The install boundary: a dependency's install lifecycle scripts run before any code this repository writes, so which of them may run is a declared contract.
The record boundary: an advisory verdict and the built artefact are recorded as evidence a reviewer can read, not as a status line in a log.

threats.scenario: A workflow action is referenced by a moving tag, so a release step's code can change without any change in this repository.

mitigations.note: Every third-party action must be pinned to an immutable reference and audited for token scope.
The reviewed pin record is the artefact the gate compares against.

threats.scenario: A known advisory affects a shipped dependency and nothing in the validation chain surfaces it, so the release report claims a verified build.

mitigations.note: The advisory gate runs as a step of the validate job, deliberately outside the offline fast gate.
The SBOM records what was actually built, so the advisory verdict can be checked against a real tree.

threats.scenario: A build consumes a vendored or generated input from a checkout that was never reviewed, so the shipped artefact cannot be traced to an approved source.

mitigations.note: The provenance check compares each vendored input against the reviewed revision record and fails on a mismatch.
The same scan that keeps values out of the tree also runs over the build output, so a vendored input cannot smuggle one in.

threats.scenario: A newly published dependency version adds an install lifecycle script, so installing the tree runs code that was never reviewed.

mitigations.note: The audit compares installed manifests with the allowlist and the workspace build permission, and fails closed when the tree is not a pnpm install.
The runbook records what a new allowance means before anyone adds one.

review_items: Has a dependency been added or bumped without re-running the advisory gate against the new tree?
Does a new workflow step run an action that is not in the reviewed pin record?
Can the SBOM still be generated offline, and does a failing generation stop the release rather than warn?
